cards.text: This psalm is from David, Israel's king, and he opens LOUD: "Blessed be the LORD, my Rock, who trains my hands for war, my fingers for battle." Nobody ever trained MY hands, friend. The mustache just showed up one day and started packing cookie boxes.
Then David stacks up names for the LORD like he's loading a cookie box: steadfast love, fortress, stronghold, deliverer, shield. The LORD is the One "in whom I take refuge."

cards.question: Fortress, stronghold, shield. David names the LORD as the One who keeps him ___.
True or false: In Psalm 144, David says the LORD keeps him far away from battle.

cards.text: Then the psalm turns. David stops talking about the LORD's strength and looks at people instead: "O LORD, what is man, that You regard him, the son of man that You think of him?"

cards.question: True or false: In Psalm 144, David asks the LORD why He has forgotten people.

cards.text: Then David says man is like a breath. I sat in a junk drawer for YEARS thinking that was forever, and David calls a whole life one breath. ONE.

cards.question: David also says a person's days are like a passing shadow. What's he saying about life?

cards.text: Then David goes BIG and asks the LORD to part His heavens, come down, and touch the mountains so they smoke. Me, when I need help, I ask somebody to hand me a spatula.

cards.question: David asks the LORD to flash His lightning and shoot His arrows. What does he want them to do?

cards.text: Then David asks the LORD to reach down from on high, set him free, and rescue him from the deep waters.

cards.question: David also asks to be rescued from the grasp of foreigners. What does he say about them?

cards.text: And right in the middle of all that rescue talk, David stops and makes the LORD a promise.

cards.question: In Psalm 144, what does David promise to give the LORD?
True or false: David says he'll make music to God on a harp of ten strings.
David sings to the One who gives victory to kings. What does he say the LORD frees His servant David from?

cards.text: Then David prays that line again: "Set me free and rescue me from the grasp of foreigners, whose mouths speak falsehood, whose right hands are deceitful." When you REALLY need help, friend, you say it twice.
Then David starts picturing life for his people. And he starts at home, with the sons and daughters.

cards.question: David says the sons will be like plants nurtured in their youth. What's that picture?
True or false: David pictures the daughters like corner pillars carved to adorn a palace.

cards.text: Then the farm report comes in, and it's GOOD: storehouses full of every kind of produce, and flocks in the tens of thousands. I used to get excited when Mother Miller could afford ONE new cookie cutter.

cards.question: In David's picture, the oxen bear great loads. What does that tell you?
Then David pictures the city walls. What does he see in them?
True or false: In David's picture, the people go off into captivity.
At the very end of Psalm 144, David says the people are blessed whose ___ is the LORD.

cards.text: "Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD." David starts this psalm with "Blessed" and ends it with "Blessed," and friend, I'll take a double batch of THAT any day.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 2 quotes "in whom I take refuge.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The joke says the mustache "just showed up one day." That contradicts his backstory, where he was already "one small cookie stamper with a big French mustache" in the bakery's bin before the Millers bought him.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: Card 1 already quoted Psalm 144:1 in full ("who trains my hands for war, my fingers for battle"). That gives away this true or false card about whether the LORD keeps David far from battle. The card also jumps back to verse 1 just to quiz what was already told.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: Card 5 quotes Psalm 144:3 word for word ("that You regard him... that You think of him"). That gives away the answer to this card, which asks whether David says the LORD has forgotten people.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The card says "David calls a whole life one breath. ONE." Psalm 144:4 says "Man is like a breath." The retelling drops the "like," changes "man" to "a whole life," and turns "a breath" into an emphatic "ONE" that is credited to David instead of kept inside Papa Dorin's own joke.
The emphatic "ONE" exaggerates what the text says and puts that exaggeration in David's mouth, not in Papa Dorin's own joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The right answer "Scatter and rout" is the text's own wording, and "rout" is Bible-sounding diction. The wrong answers ("Light up the sky", "Mark a safe path") are plain modern phrases, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The card says David "makes the LORD a promise," and card 2 asks what David "promise[s] to give the LORD." Psalm 144:9 says "I will sing to You a new song." The text never calls this a promise.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The true or false card about a "harp of ten strings" asks the baker to confirm a detail they have never been given and can't reason out. It is a coin flip, and it follows a discovery question (card 2) with no context in between.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess a wording detail ("the deadly sword" against "the lion's mouth" or "the king's spear") with no story card giving context. This is the same kind of detail guess as the Psalm 23 bad example ("oil, myrrh or perfume?"). It is the third choice card in a row in this stretch that relies on luck.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The true or false statement is the exact detail from verse 12 ("corner pillars carved to adorn a palace"). The baker has nothing to reason from and can only guess whether this wording is in the psalm. The card doesn't ask what the picture means.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank is verse 15 quoted with one word missing ("blessed whose ___ is the LORD"). It tests the wording of the line, not meaning the baker can reason out. The wrong answers "wealth" and "harvest" also make little sense in that sentence.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.
